case_analysis.focal_point: Whether 18 U.S.C. § 666(a)(1)(B) criminalizes acceptance of after-the-fact gratuities (rewards) by covered state/local/tribal officials, or is limited to quid-pro-quo bribes intended to influence an official act or decision.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 18 U.S.C. § 666(a)(1)(B) (federal-program bribery statute: prohibits certain officials of agencies receiving >$10,000 in federal benefits from corruptly soliciting/accepting things of value intending to be influenced or rewarded in connection with agency business involving $5,000+).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Snyder argues § 666 is a bribery statute, not an all-purpose ethics code, and should be construed to reach only quid-pro-quo bribery—payments made with an intent to influence specific official action—because reading the word "rewarded" to cover mere gratuities (after-the-fact tips/thanks without an agreement to influence) would: (1) expand federal criminal jurisdiction deep into traditional state and local governance; (2) create vagueness and due-process notice problems by making ordinary political or constituent interactions potentially felonious; (3) conflict with this Court’s narrowing trend for public-corruption statutes (rule of lenity, federalism, separation of powers concerns); and (4) effectively circumvent limits this Court has imposed on federal corruption theories by allowing prosecutors to repackage non-quid-pro-quo conduct as a federal felony whenever the agency receives federal funds.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The United States argues § 666’s text covers not only bribes but also gratuities because Congress expressly prohibited payments accepted "intending to be influenced or rewarded," and "rewarded" naturally includes after-the-fact compensation for past favorable treatment; the statute’s other limiting elements (corrupt intent; nexus to agency business/transactions worth $5,000+; and the federal-benefits threshold) sufficiently cabin its scope; and a broader construction is consistent with Congress’s purpose to protect the integrity of federally funded entities from corruption in forms that include both prospective influence and retrospective payoff.

John Roberts.reasoning: The Government’s best argument remains textual—Congress added “or rewarded,” and in isolation that can reach post hoc payments—but the statute’s full mens rea (“corruptly” and “intending to be influenced”) reads most naturally as requiring a quid pro quo, with “rewarded” doing work to cover deferred payoffs rather than free-floating gratuities. Justice Kagan’s surplusage point is decisive for me: if “rewarded” alone creates a gratuities offense, “to be influenced” and much of “corruptly” lose independent limiting force in a criminal statute. Justice Sotomayor’s fair-notice and line-drawing concerns reinforce the federalism-sensitive clear-statement principle: absent language like § 201(c), we should not treat § 666 as a broad federal ethics code for state and local officials tied only to federal funding. Sun-Diamond’s bribe/gratuity distinction fits comfortably with this narrower construction and supports rejecting the Government’s attempt to collapse the categories without clearer text.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Government’s strongest argument is that adding “or rewarded” naturally reaches after-the-fact gratuities, but the original public meaning of the full phrase—accepting something of value “corruptly” and “intending to be influenced or rewarded”—still denotes a corrupt exchange, including a payoff delivered later, not a unilateral token of thanks. As Justice Kagan explains, treating “rewarded” as a standalone gratuity theory creates a surplusage problem by largely nullifying “intending to be influenced” and diluting “corruptly” into an empty incantation. Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Alito are also right that the broader reading would effectively federalize state and local ethics whenever federal funds are present, a major intrusion we should not presume absent a clear statement like the distinct gratuities provision in § 201(c) recognized in Sun-Diamond. With that structure and federalism backdrop, any residual ambiguity in this criminal statute is resolved by a narrow construction and lenity, so I remain with the Petitioner.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The Government’s best point remains the addition of “or rewarded,” but reading that as a standalone gratuities hook cannot be reconciled with the statute’s surrounding mens rea—“corruptly” and “intending to be influenced”—which, as Chief Justice Roberts notes, are classic markers of an exchange rather than mere appreciation. Justice Kagan’s surplusage concern reinforces that the Government’s view would largely nullify “to be influenced” and drain “corruptly” of limiting force, effectively turning § 666 into an expansive federal ethics code for state and local officials whenever federal funds are present. Sun-Diamond, as multiple colleagues emphasize (Roberts, Thomas), cautions against blurring the bribe/gratuity line absent clear textual signals like those Congress used in § 201(c), and any remaining ambiguity in this criminal statute should be resolved narrowly given federalism and fair-notice consequences. I therefore remain with Petitioner and read “rewarded” to capture timing within a quid pro quo (including deferred payoffs), not to eliminate the exchange requirement.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The Government’s strongest textual point is that Congress added “or rewarded,” which could be read to reach after-the-fact gratuities, but that reading becomes untenable once we take seriously the rest of the mens rea package—“corruptly” and “intending to be influenced”—which, as Justice Kagan explains, would otherwise be largely surplusage and would drain “corruptly” of its exchange-limiting force. Chief Justice Roberts’s federalism and fair-notice concerns matter in a pragmatic way: without a quid pro quo requirement, § 666 risks turning commonplace post hoc gift-giving around local government interactions into a federal felony, inviting arbitrary enforcement that predictably falls hardest on the least resourced defendants. Sun-Diamond’s bribe/gratuity distinction reinforces that when Congress wants a gratuities offense, it legislates clearer boundaries (as in § 201(c)); absent that clarity here, lenity and a federalism-sensitive construction support reading “rewarded” to cover deferred payoffs within a corrupt bargain rather than standalone gratitude. Nothing in colleagues’ exchanges undermines that this narrower construction still allows prosecution of genuine corruption while preventing overbroad criminalization.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The Government’s strongest point remains the bare-text claim that adding “or rewarded” must reach after-the-fact gratuities; but read with the full mens rea—“corruptly” and “intending to be influenced”—that would dilute the exchange-signaling function of “corruptly” and create a surplusage problem for “to be influenced” in a criminal statute. Chief Justice Roberts’s federalism and fair-notice concerns sharpen the practical stakes: a gratuities reading risks turning § 666 into a roving federal ethics code for state/local officials whenever federal funds are in the background, without the kind of explicit, bounded gratuities provision Congress used in § 201(c) (as Sun-Diamond underscores). Justice Barrett’s emphasis that “rewarded” can still do work on a quid-pro-quo reading (capturing deferred payoffs pursuant to an understanding) preserves statutory coherence while leaving genuine corruption prosecutable. Nothing in colleagues’ analyses undercuts the core textual/structural point that “rewarded” is best read as about timing within an exchange, not elimination of the exchange requirement.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The Government’s best point remains the textual addition of “or rewarded,” but even on its own terms that word must be read with the rest of the mens rea—“corruptly” and “intending to be influenced”—which, as the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize, speaks the language of a bargain rather than an unprompted token of gratitude. If “rewarded” silently created a distinct gratuities offense, we would expect Congress to supply the kind of limiting architecture it used in § 201(c), and Sun-Diamond’s bribe/gratuity distinction makes that expectation more, not less, reasonable. I also find persuasive Justice Roberts’s and Justice Sotomayor’s federalism and fair-notice concerns: absent a clear statement, we should not construe § 666 to federalize vast swaths of state and local ethics whenever federal funds appear in the background, and any residual ambiguity in this criminal statute is resolved by lenity. On the best textual and structural reading, “rewarded” does work by capturing the timing of a quid pro quo (including deferred payoffs) without eliminating the exchange requirement.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The Government’s best textual point remains that “rewarded” can naturally describe an after-the-fact gratuity, but as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, that term must be read with “corruptly” and “intending to be influenced,” which are classic quid-pro-quo markers; otherwise “to be influenced” becomes largely surplusage and “corruptly” loses limiting force. Justice Sotomayor’s fair-notice and line-drawing concerns—and the federalism implications Roberts highlights—matter a great deal here: absent a clear statement, we should not transform § 666 into a broad federal ethics code for state and local officials whenever federal funds are in the background. Sun-Diamond’s bribe/gratuity distinction supports keeping gratuities as a separately and expressly defined offense (as in § 201(c)), and any residual ambiguity in this criminal statute should be resolved narrowly. “Rewarded” still does work on our reading by covering deferred payoffs pursuant to a corrupt understanding, so the narrower construction is both textually coherent and institutionally prudent.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The Government’s strongest point remains the disjunctive “influenced or rewarded,” which in isolation could be read to reach gratuities, but the phrase cannot be severed from the statute’s mens rea (“corruptly” and “intending”) and its tie to a specific “business, transaction, or series of transactions.” As Justice Kagan emphasizes, treating “rewarded” as a freestanding gratuities hook would create a serious surplusage problem by largely collapsing “to be influenced” and draining “corruptly” of its exchange-signaling work in a criminal statute. Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas further underscore why that reading is especially suspect here: it would effectively federalize state and local gift/ethics regulation based on federal-funds eligibility without the clearer gratuities architecture Congress used in § 201(c), and Sun-Diamond’s bribe/gratuity distinction supports construing § 666 narrowly to require a quid pro quo (including deferred payment pursuant to an understanding). Nothing in the colleagues’ precedent discussion undermines that textual, federalism-sensitive, and lenity-consistent interpretation, so I remain with Petitioner.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The Government’s strongest point remains the plain-language pull of “or rewarded,” but, as Justice Kagan explains, reading that word to create a freestanding gratuities offense collapses the surrounding mens rea—“corruptly” and “intending to be influenced”—into surplusage or an empty label. Chief Justice Roberts’s federalism and fair-notice concerns underscore the practical consequences: the broader reading would function as an unadministrable federal ethics code for state and local officials whenever federal funds are somewhere in the background, sweeping in routine post hoc gifts absent any corrupt agreement. Sun-Diamond reinforces that Congress typically draws a clearer line when it criminalizes gratuities, and “rewarded” still does work on a bribery/quid-pro-quo reading by capturing deferred payoffs pursuant to a prior corrupt understanding. Nothing raised in conference undermines that narrower construction, so I remain with Petitioner.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 666(a)(1)(B) must be read as a bribery statute requiring a quid pro quo, because its operative mens rea—accepting something of value “corruptly” and “intending to be influenced”—is the traditional marker of an exchange rather than a mere after-the-fact token of appreciation. Reading “rewarded” to federalize gratuities would substantially expand federal criminal jurisdiction into state and local governance and raise serious notice and federalism concerns; where Congress has not spoken with clarity, the Court should avoid that construction and adhere to the narrowest grounds consistent with the statute. This Court’s distinction between bribes and gratuities in § 201 underscores that bribery requires a quid pro quo, while gratuities are a different, expressly delineated offense; importing gratuities into § 666 without similarly clear limits would blur that line. Consistent with institutional legitimacy and restrained interpretation, the better reading confines § 666 to quid-pro-quo bribery in connection with qualifying agency business.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The text of § 666(a)(1)(B) must be read as a bribery prohibition requiring a corrupt quid pro quo: the statute’s mens rea term “corruptly” is the traditional marker of an exchange—accepting value in return for official action—rather than mere after-the-fact gifts. Reading “rewarded” to criminalize gratuities would transform § 666 into a sweeping federal ethics code over state and local officials whenever an entity receives federal funds, raising serious federalism and notice concerns that counsel a narrowing construction and, at minimum, application of the rule of lenity. Consistent with Sun-Diamond’s distinction between bribes and gratuities, “rewarded” is best understood as describing the official’s intent in a bribery scheme (payment promised or understood as compensation for official favor) rather than extending § 666 to untethered, retrospective gratuities. Because Congress knows how to criminalize gratuities expressly (cf. 18 U.S.C. § 201(c)), § 666 should be confined to quid-pro-quo bribery in connection with agency business involving $5,000 or more.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 666(a)(1)(B) must be read as a bribery statute: its requirement that an official act "corruptly" and accept something of value "intending to be influenced or rewarded" is best understood to demand a quid pro quo, not mere after-the-fact gratitude, because otherwise "corruptly" does little work and the statute becomes an open-ended federal ethics code for state and local officials. As this Court stressed in Sun-Diamond, federal corruption statutes should not be stretched to cover generalized gratuities absent a clear tie to a specific corrupt exchange; treating any post hoc "reward" as a felony would blur the settled bribe/gratuity line and invite overbroad prosecutions. Given the serious federalism and fair-notice concerns that follow from the Government’s expansive construction, any residual ambiguity in § 666 should be resolved narrowly under the rule of lenity. The more reasonable textual reading is that "rewarded" captures the payoff aspect of a corrupt bargain (including payment after performance), not a standalone gratuity without an agreement to influence an identified transaction.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 666(a)(1)(B) should be read as a bribery statute requiring a quid pro quo—an agreement to influence official action—because expanding it to after-the-fact gratuities would federalize routine state and local ethics matters and create serious notice and line-drawing problems inconsistent with due process and fair administration of criminal law. Although the statute includes the word “rewarded,” the requirement that the official act “corruptly” and the Court’s insistence on limiting public-corruption crimes to clearly defined exchanges counsel a narrowing construction, especially where the broader reading risks sweeping in ordinary tokens of appreciation. As in Sun-Diamond, the traditional distinction between bribes and gratuities matters, and criminal liability should not attach without a specific, concrete nexus to an agreed-upon official act or decision. Applying the rule of lenity and federalism-sensitive interpretation, § 666 should be limited to quid-pro-quo bribery rather than covering mere rewards.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 666(a)(1)(B) requires that the official act "corruptly" and accept something of value "intending to be influenced or rewarded" in connection with covered agency business, and reading "rewarded" to reach mere after-the-fact gratuities risks collapsing that mens rea into an amorphous ethics code with serious workability and federalism consequences. Consistent with Sun-Diamond’s bribery/gratuity distinction, the better textual coherence is to treat the statute’s “influenced or rewarded” phrase as capturing the timing of a quid pro quo (payment before or after), not eliminating the exchange requirement. Otherwise, “intending to be influenced” does little independent work because prosecutors could proceed on “rewarded” without proving any agreement, contrary to the Court’s insistence that bribery entails a quid pro quo. Given the ambiguity and the statute’s significant expansion into state and local governance, a narrowing construction limiting § 666 to quid-pro-quo bribery is the more workable reading.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 666(a)(1)(B) is best read, by its text and structure, as a bribery prohibition requiring a quid pro quo: an official must act “corruptly” and accept something of value “intending to be influenced” in connection with agency business, language that naturally targets exchanges rather than mere after-the-fact tokens. Reading “rewarded” to criminalize gratuities would risk collapsing the statute into a sweeping federal ethics code for state and local officials whenever their agencies receive federal funds, raising serious federalism and fair-notice concerns better avoided absent a clear statement from Congress. This Court has emphasized that bribery turns on a quid pro quo—“a specific intent to give or receive something of value in exchange for an official act”—as distinguished from gratuities, United States v. Sun-Diamond Growers, 526 U.S. 398, 404–05 (1999), and any remaining ambiguity in § 666 should be resolved under the rule of lenity. On that reading, “rewarded” can be understood to capture payments contemplated as part of an exchange (including deferred compensation), not unilateral after-the-fact gifts lacking any agreement to influence official action.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 666(a)(1)(B) should be read as a bribery statute limited to quid-pro-quo corruption, not an open-ended federal ethics code for state and local officials, because expanding it to after-the-fact gratuities would push federal criminal law deep into traditional state and local governance without clear congressional authorization. Although the statute includes the word “rewarded,” that term can naturally refer to the receipt of a thing of value as part of a corrupt exchange—i.e., a payoff for an understanding—rather than mere thanks after the fact, and the rule of lenity counsels against the broader reading in a criminal statute. This Court’s public-corruption cases have repeatedly insisted on clear limiting principles to preserve workability and fair notice, and Sun-Diamond’s distinction between bribes and gratuities underscores that gratuity liability is a distinct, more expansive theory that Congress typically addresses explicitly (as in § 201(c)), not by implication in § 666. A quid-pro-quo construction better fits judicial restraint, protects due-process notice, and avoids transforming commonplace constituent interactions into federal felonies whenever an entity receives federal funds.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 666(a)(1)(B) requires that the official act “corruptly” and with intent “to be influenced or rewarded,” language that, read in context and consistent with the ordinary distinction between bribery and gratuities, most naturally targets quid-pro-quo exchanges rather than mere after-the-fact gifts. Interpreting “rewarded” to criminalize gratuities risks collapsing “to be influenced” into surplusage and turning § 666 into a broad federal ethics code for state and local officials, an implausible intrusion absent clearer text; methodological consistency and the rule of lenity counsel a narrower construction. This Court has emphasized that bribery entails a quid pro quo—“a specific intent to give or receive something of value in exchange for an official act”—as contrasted with illegal gratuities, United States v. Sun-Diamond Growers of Cal., 526 U.S. 398, 404–05 (1999), and nothing in § 666 unmistakably indicates Congress meant to criminalize gratuities without an exchange. Given federalism-sensitive criminal statutes, we should not extend § 666 beyond bribery absent unambiguous language.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 666(a)(1)(B) is best read as a bribery provision limited to quid-pro-quo corruption, because its use of “corruptly” and the phrase “intending to be influenced” align it with § 201(b)’s bribery framework rather than § 201(c)’s separate illegal-gratuity regime. As Sun-Diamond Growers instructs, bribery requires a specific quid pro quo—an intent to exchange something of value for an official act—whereas gratuities are punished only when Congress clearly creates that distinct offense with a different mens rea and limiting structure, which § 666 does not do. Reading “rewarded” to federalize after-the-fact gifts without an agreement risks vagueness and disproportionate practical consequences by turning ordinary local interactions into federal felonies, contrary to fair-notice and federalism-sensitive construction (and the rule of lenity in close cases). The statute can still reach post-payment “rewards” when they are part of, or evidence of, an earlier corrupt agreement, but not mere gratuities absent a quid pro quo.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether 18 U.S.C. § 666(a)(1)(B) criminalizes state and local officials’ acceptance of after-the-fact “gratuities” (rewards) absent an agreement to be influenced (i.e., a bribe), or instead is limited to bribery-type quid pro quo corruption.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 18 U.S.C. § 666(a)(1)(B) (federal-program bribery statute governing agents of state/local/tribal entities receiving significant federal benefits).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Snyder argues that § 666(a)(1)(B) should be read to cover only bribes—payments accepted corruptly as part of a quid pro quo to influence an official act or government business—and not mere gratuities given as a reward after the fact without any prior agreement. He contends that the Seventh Circuit’s broader reading (covering ‘influenced or rewarded’) effectively federalizes state/local ethics and gift issues, creates vagueness and due-process notice problems because ordinary gifts or political support can be criminalized without a clear quid pro quo, and raises serious federalism and separation-of-powers concerns by expanding federal criminal jurisdiction into traditional state and local governance. Amici echo these points, emphasizing strict construction of criminal statutes, the rule of lenity, and constitutional avoidance (First Amendment/political activity spillover and structural limits).
case_analysis.respondent_position: The United States argues that § 666(a)(1)(B)’s text—prohibiting corrupt acceptance of a thing of value ‘intending to be influenced or rewarded’—covers not only classic bribes (influence) but also corrupt gratuities (rewards) tied to government business, so long as the defendant acted ‘corruptly’ and with the requisite intent. The government maintains that including ‘rewarded’ reflects Congress’s deliberate choice to reach after-the-fact payments connected to official business, that the ‘corruptly’ element meaningfully limits the statute to wrongful transactions rather than innocent gifts, and that the statute’s purpose (protecting the integrity of federally funded programs and entities receiving significant federal benefits) supports a broader construction.

John Roberts.reasoning: The government’s strongest point remains the textual force of “rewarded,” but as Justice Kagan and Justice Gorsuch stress, that word cannot be read in isolation from “corruptly” and the specific-intent clause; otherwise we effectively create a free-standing federal gratuities offense for state/local officials without the clearer “for or because of” structure Congress used in § 201. Sun-Diamond’s insistence on administrable limits and a concrete nexus in federal corruption crimes reinforces that we should not collapse the bribe/gratuity line by letting “rewarded” do all the work while rendering “corruptly” nearly surplus. Justice Barrett’s framing—that “rewarded” can still have meaning within a quid-pro-quo framework by capturing payments in an ongoing or implicit corrupt arrangement—offers the narrowest construction that gives each term work while avoiding a sweeping federal ethics code. Given the federalism and fair-notice stakes in § 666’s reach, any lingering ambiguity should be resolved narrowly under lenity.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The respondent’s best textual point is that Congress included “rewarded,” but that word cannot be read in isolation to create a gratuities offense when the statute also requires the defendant act “corruptly” and with intent “to be influenced or rewarded” in connection with government business; in ordinary legal usage, that mens rea signals an exchange-like misuse of office, not mere after-the-fact appreciation. Justice Gorsuch’s emphasis that the mens rea must do real work is decisive under a textualist approach: if “rewarded” alone sweeps in any later gift, “corruptly” becomes largely surplusage and § 666 expands far beyond its anti-bribery function. Justice Kagan’s point about § 201 is also significant: where Congress intended to criminalize gratuities, it spoke distinctly and clearly (“for or because of”), and we should not silently import that regime into § 666 with its serious federalism and fair-notice consequences. Given remaining ambiguity in a criminal statute, lenity confirms the narrower, quid-pro-quo construction.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The respondent’s best textual point is that Congress added “rewarded,” and we should not read it out; but that word cannot be severed from the statute’s requirement that the payment be accepted “corruptly,” which in ordinary criminal-law usage connotes an exchange-like misuse of office rather than mere after-the-fact gratitude. Chief Justice Roberts’s federalism and fair-notice concerns reinforce the practical consequences of the broader construction: absent the clearer “for or because of” gratuities language Congress used in § 201, reading § 666 as a sweeping gratuities regime would federalize state/local gift-ethics and invite uncertain prosecutions. Justice Kagan and Justice Gorsuch persuasively explain that “rewarded” still does work within a quid pro quo framework (including ongoing arrangements) without collapsing the Sun-Diamond bribe/gratuity line or rendering “corruptly” surplusage. With residual ambiguity in a criminal statute of this structural breadth, lenity properly confirms the bribery-only reading.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The government’s strongest point is the textual one: Congress added “rewarded,” and we should give it meaning beyond pre-agreement bribery. But as Justice Kagan and Justice Gorsuch underscore, reading “rewarded” to create a standalone gratuities offense collapses Sun-Diamond’s bribe/gratuity line and effectively nullifies “corruptly,” inviting vague, discretionary enforcement in ways that will predictably burden less powerful state and local officials. Chief Justice Roberts’s federalism and fair-notice concern reinforces that, absent a clear statement like § 201’s distinct gratuities language, we should not turn § 666 into a sweeping federal ethics code covering after-the-fact gifts. “Rewarded” can still do work within a quid pro quo framework by capturing ongoing or implicit exchange arrangements, so the narrower construction best harmonizes text, mens rea, and administrable limits.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest move is textual—“influenced or rewarded” must mean something, and “rewarded” can naturally include post hoc gifts—but that reading cannot be severed from the statute’s requirement that the official act “corruptly” and “intend[]” influence/reward in connection with specific government business, which points to an exchange-like misuse of office rather than mere gratitude. Chief Justice Roberts’s federalism/notice concern sharpens the practical consequence: if “rewarded” alone creates a gratuities offense, § 666 becomes an open-ended federal ethics code for state/local officials without the clearer gratuities language Congress used in § 201. Justice Barrett’s point is persuasive that “rewarded” still does work within a quid-pro-quo framework (capturing payments in an ongoing or implicit corrupt arrangement), preserving textual meaning without collapsing the bribe/gratuity line. Sun-Diamond, as Justice Gorsuch emphasizes, supports demanding a concrete transactional nexus in corruption crimes, and any remaining ambiguity in this criminal statute is resolved by lenity.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The government’s strongest point remains the bare word “rewarded,” but as Justice Kagan explains, we cannot treat that single word as silently importing § 201’s separate gratuities regime when § 666 instead requires the defendant to act “corruptly” and to accept value “intending to be influenced or rewarded” in connection with covered business—language that, in ordinary legal usage, connotes an exchange-like misuse of office. Chief Justice Roberts’s federalism and fair-notice concerns reinforce the need for a clear statement before transforming § 666 into a general federal ethics code for state and local officials, especially given the felony penalties and the statute’s breadth. Sun-Diamond’s insistence on administrable limits in federal corruption crimes supports reading “rewarded” to do work within a quid pro quo framework (including ongoing arrangements) rather than collapsing bribery and gratuities. With any residual ambiguity in this criminal statute, lenity and constitutional avoidance confirm the narrower, bribery-like construction.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The respondent’s best textual point is that § 666 says “influenced or rewarded,” which at first glance could reach after-the-fact payments; but that word cannot be read in isolation from “corruptly” and the intent clause, which together traditionally signal an exchange-like misuse of office rather than mere appreciation. Chief Justice Roberts’s federalism and fair-notice concerns reinforce the institutional and practical problem with a broad gratuities reading: it would effectively federalize state/local gift-ethics rules without the clear congressional statement we ordinarily require in criminal statutes with major structural consequences. Justice Kagan and Justice Barrett persuasively explain how “rewarded” can still do work within a quid pro quo framework (including ongoing or implicit arrangements) without silently importing § 201’s distinct gratuities regime, and Sun-Diamond’s bribe/gratuity distinction supports maintaining a coherent, administrable line. Given lingering ambiguity in a criminal statute, lenity and institutional caution counsel the narrower bribery-type construction.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest point remains the bare word “rewarded,” which in isolation can cover post hoc gratuities; but as Justice Gorsuch and Justice Kagan emphasize, the statute’s mens rea (“corruptly” and “intending to be influenced or rewarded”) is most naturally read as an exchange-like intent tied to identified government business, not mere appreciation. Chief Justice Roberts’s federalism and fair-notice concern matters under a textualist approach because it highlights how implausible it is that Congress would silently transform § 666 into a sweeping gift-ethics code for state and local officials when, in § 201, it drew the bribery/gratuity line expressly with distinct “for or because of” language. Sun-Diamond’s insistence on administrable limits and a concrete transactional nexus reinforces that we should not collapse bribery and gratuities without clear text, and any residual ambiguity in this criminal statute is resolved by lenity. I therefore maintain the bribery-type quid pro quo construction while giving “rewarded” work to do within ongoing or implicit corrupt arrangements.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The government’s strongest point remains the textual insistence that “rewarded” must add coverage for after-the-fact payments, but that reading becomes untenable once we give “corruptly” its ordinary limiting function in anti-bribery law—signaling misuse of office in an exchange-like relationship rather than criminalizing mere gratitude. Justice Kagan’s comparison to § 201 is especially persuasive: Congress knew how to create a distinct gratuities offense using “for or because of” language, and § 666’s different structure and mens rea make it implausible that Congress silently federalized a broad state/local gift-ethics regime. Chief Justice Roberts’s federalism and fair-notice concerns, reinforced by Sun-Diamond’s insistence on administrable limits and a clear bribe/gratuity line, underscore the practical consequences of the broader construction: it risks vagueness and arbitrary enforcement. If any ambiguity persists after harmonizing “rewarded” with “corruptly,” lenity properly resolves it in favor of the narrower, bribery-type quid pro quo interpretation.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 666(a)(1)(B) should be construed, consistent with narrow decisionmaking and federalism concerns, to reach bribery-type quid pro quo corruption rather than after-the-fact “rewards” untethered to any agreement to influence official action. Reading “rewarded” to sweep in gratuities risks collapsing the established bribe/gratuity distinction and invites the kind of overbroad federal criminalization of state and local gift/ethics matters that raises serious due-process notice concerns—concerns this Court has addressed by insisting on a concrete link to official action in the analogous federal gratuities context. See 18 U.S.C. § 666(a)(1)(B); United States v. Sun-Diamond Growers of Cal., 526 U.S. 398, 404–05 (1999). Where statutory text and structure leave doubt about criminal liability, the Court should adopt the narrower construction that avoids constitutional and federalism problems rather than expand federal jurisdiction into traditional state governance.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The text of 18 U.S.C. § 666(a)(1)(B) criminalizes an agent’s corrupt acceptance of value “intending to be influenced or rewarded” in connection with government business, but read in light of ordinary meaning and the statute’s anti-bribery focus, “corruptly” and the intent clause require a quid pro quo—an agreement to be influenced—rather than mere after-the-fact gifts. Construing “rewarded” to sweep in gratuities would effectively federalize state and local ethics rules, expanding federal criminal jurisdiction beyond the statute’s clear meaning and raising serious federalism and fair-notice concerns, so the rule of lenity counsels a narrower reading. Our approach in United States v. Sun-Diamond Growers of California, 526 U.S. 398 (1999), distinguishing bribery from gratuities and insisting on a tight nexus to the prohibited exchange, supports limiting § 666 to bribery-type corruption rather than open-ended criminalization of rewards. Accordingly, § 666(a)(1)(B) should be interpreted to reach quid pro quo bribery, not standalone gratuities.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 666(a)(1)(B) is a criminal statute that, read in context and in light of its traditional anti-corruption focus, is best limited to bribery-type quid pro quo transactions rather than after-the-fact “rewards” untethered to an agreement to be influenced. Although the phrase “intending to be influenced or rewarded” includes the word “rewarded,” the statute’s requirement that the defendant act “corruptly” is most naturally read to demand an exchange-like intent—consistent with Sun-Diamond’s insistence that bribery involves a quid pro quo and that expansive readings risk criminalizing ordinary gift-giving without clear notice. A broader gratuities construction would substantially federalize state and local ethics rules and invite uncertain, consequence-laden prosecutions based on ambiguous post hoc “thanks,” so the rule of lenity counsels the narrower reading. This interpretation preserves § 666’s core function—targeting quid pro quo corruption affecting federally funded entities—without converting it into a general federal gratuities code.
